Physiology 03.question: ১) Average daily secretion of gastric juice..?
Physiology 03.exp:
The average daily secretion of gastric juice in an adult human is approximately 1500 mL/day. Gastric juice is secreted by the gastric glands of the stomach and contains hydrochloric acid (HCl), pepsinogen, mucus, intrinsic factor, and water. HCl helps in protein digestion by activating pepsinogen to pepsin and provides an acidic environment for enzyme activity. Gastric secretion is regulated mainly by gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine. The amount of gastric juice is lower than intestinal secretions but higher than salivary secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric juice: ≈ 1500 mL/day

  • Saliva: ≈ 1500 mL/day

  • Pancreatic juice: ≈ 1500 mL/day

  • Bile: ≈ 500–1000 mL/day

  • Main acid in gastric juice: HCl

  • Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells

Exam Pearl:
Average daily gastric juice secretion in adults is about 1.5 liters (1500 mL).

Physiology 03.question: ২) Enteropeptidase is a proteolytic enzyme which is a component of…?
Physiology 03.exp:
Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) is a proteolytic enzyme present in the brush border membrane of the duodenum and is a component of succus entericus (intestinal juice). Its main function is to activate trypsinogen (inactive pancreatic enzyme) into trypsin. Activated trypsin then converts other pancreatic zymogens into their active forms, allowing protein digestion in the small intestine.

It is not a component of saliva or gastric juice. Although pancreatic juice contains trypsinogen and other proteolytic enzymes, it does not contain enteropeptidase.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Enteropeptidase → Duodenal brush border enzyme

  • Activates trypsinogen → trypsin

  • Trypsin activates other pancreatic zymogens

  • Component of succus entericus

Exam Pearl:
Enteropeptidase of intestinal juice initiates pancreatic protein digestion by activating trypsinogen.

Physiology 03.question: ৩) Trypsinogen is activated by which of the following?
Physiology 03.exp:
Trypsinogen is an inactive pancreatic proteolytic enzyme (zymogen) secreted by pancreatic acinar cells. It is activated in the duodenum by enteropeptidase (enterokinase), an enzyme present on the intestinal brush border. Enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen → trypsin. The newly formed trypsin then activates more trypsinogen molecules and other pancreatic zymogens such as chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, and elastase.

Gastric HCl helps activate pepsinogen to pepsin but does not activate trypsinogen. Trypsin can activate trypsinogen, but the initial activation is performed by enteropeptidase.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Trypsinogen activation: Enteropeptidase (duodenum)

  • Trypsinogen → Trypsin

  • Trypsin activates:

    • Chymotrypsinogen → Chymotrypsin

    • Procarboxypeptidase → Carboxypeptidase

    • Proelastase → Elastase

Exam Pearl:
Enteropeptidase is the enzyme that starts pancreatic protease activation by converting trypsinogen into trypsin.

Physiology 03.question: ৪) Which cell secretes pepsinogen?
Physiology 03.exp:
Chief cells (zymogenic cells) of the gastric glands secrete pepsinogen, which is an inactive precursor (zymogen) of the proteolytic enzyme pepsin. In the acidic environment of the stomach, HCl secreted by parietal (oxyntic) cells converts pepsinogen into active pepsin, which helps digest proteins into smaller peptides.

Oxyntic (parietal) cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor, not pepsinogen. Mucus neck cells produce mucus for protection of the gastric mucosa, and G cells secrete gastrin, which stimulates gastric acid secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Chief cell → Pepsinogen

  • Parietal/Oxyntic cell → HCl + Intrinsic factor

  • Mucous neck cell → Mucus

  • G cell → Gastrin

  • HCl converts pepsinogen → pepsin

Exam Pearl:
Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; parietal cells provide HCl to activate it into pepsin.

Physiology 03.question: ৫) Which is not true about ecbolic secretion?
Physiology 03.exp:
Ecbolic secretion refers to the enzyme-rich secretion of the pancreas produced by pancreatic acinar cells. It is stimulated mainly by cholecystokinin (CCK), which is released from the duodenum in response to fatty food and amino acids. Therefore, options stating that it is enzyme-rich and occurs in response to fatty food are correct.

Secretin primarily stimulates hydrolytic (ductal) secretion, which is rich in bicarbonate and water from pancreatic duct cells, not enzyme secretion. Therefore, "stimulated by secretin" is not true for ecbolic secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ecbolic secretion → Pancreatic enzymes → Acinar cells

  • Main stimulus: CCK

  • CCK release: Fatty acids + amino acids in duodenum

  • Hydrolytic secretion → Bicarbonate-rich → Secretin mediated

  • Secretin acts mainly on pancreatic duct cells

Exam Pearl:
CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme (ecbolic) secretion, while secretin stimulates bicarbonate secretion.

Physiology 03.question: ৬) Which is not true about function of bile?
Physiology 03.exp:
Bile performs several important functions in digestion, especially in fat digestion and absorption. Bile salts decrease surface tension and act as emulsifying agents, breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets, which increases the surface area for pancreatic lipase action. Therefore, bile helps in the activation and effective action of lipase. Bile also acts as a buffer due to bicarbonate content and serves as a lubricant in the intestine. It can stimulate intestinal motility and increase peristalsis. However, bile does not increase surface tension; rather, it decreases surface tension.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bile salts → Emulsification of fat

  • Bile salts decrease surface tension

  • Facilitate action of pancreatic lipase

  • Bile contains:

    • Bile salts

    • Bile pigments

    • Cholesterol

    • Phospholipids

    • Bicarbonate

Exam Pearl:

Physiology 03.question: ৭) Specific gravity of gall bladder bile is…?
Physiology 03.exp:
The specific gravity of gall bladder bile is approximately 1.03. Bile stored in the gall bladder becomes more concentrated because the gall bladder absorbs water and electrolytes from hepatic bile. As a result, gall bladder bile contains a higher concentration of bile salts, pigments, cholesterol, and other organic substances compared with liver bile. The specific gravity of hepatic bile is lower (around 1.01), while concentrated gall bladder bile has a specific gravity around 1.03.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gall bladder bile specific gravity: ≈ 1.03

  • Gall bladder concentrates bile by absorbing:

    • Water

    • Sodium chloride

    • Other electrolytes

  • Bile salts are important for:

    • Fat emulsification

    • Fat absorption

Exam Pearl:
Gall bladder bile is concentrated bile with a specific gravity of about 1.03.

Physiology 03.question: ৮) Gastric emptying is inhibited by which of the following?
Physiology 03.exp:
Cholecystokinin-pancreozymin (CCK-PZ) is the most important hormone that inhibits gastric emptying, particularly after a fatty meal. It is secreted by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids. CCK decreases gastric motility and increases pyloric sphincter tone, allowing adequate time for fat digestion and absorption in the small intestine. It also stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

Although secretin can also slow gastric emptying, its primary role is to stimulate bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion. In standard physiology MCQs, CCK-PZ is considered the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CCK-PZ → Decreases gastric emptying

  • Secreted by I cells of duodenum and jejunum

  • Stimulated by fatty acids and amino acids

  • Also causes:

    • Gallbladder contraction

    • Pancreatic enzyme secretion

    • Relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi

Exam Pearl:
Fat in the duodenum releases CCK, which is

Physiology 03.question: ৯) Site of absorption of glucose is..?
Physiology 03.exp:
The jejunum is the principal site for glucose absorption in the small intestine. Glucose is absorbed across the apical membrane of enterocytes by the SGLT-1 (sodium-glucose cotransporter-1) through secondary active transport, driven by the sodium gradient maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. It then exits the basolateral membrane via GLUT-2 into the portal circulation. Although some glucose absorption can occur in the duodenum and ileum, the jejunum is the major site because of its extensive villi and absorptive surface area.

The liver metabolizes absorbed glucose but does not absorb it from the intestinal lumen. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major site of glucose absorption: Jejunum

  • Apical transporter: SGLT-1

  • Basolateral transporter: GLUT-2

  • Fructose is absorbed by GLUT-5 (facilitated diffusion).

  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the sodium gradient required for glucose absorption.

Exam Pearl:
Glucose is absorbed predominantly in the jejunum via the SGLT-1 sodium-glucose cotransporter.

Physiology 03.question: ১০) (Glucose + glucose) = ?
Physiology 03.exp:
Maltose is a disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α-1,4 glycosidic bond. It is produced during the digestion of starch and glycogen by the action of amylase. Maltose is subsequently hydrolyzed by the enzyme maltase in the intestinal brush border to yield two glucose molecules, which are then absorbed.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Sucrose = Glucose + Fructose

  • Lactose = Glucose + Galactose

  • Fructose is a monosaccharide, not a disaccharide.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Maltose = Glucose + Glucose

  • Sucrose = Glucose + Fructose

  • Lactose = Glucose + Galactose

  • Maltase → Maltose → 2 Glucose

  • Sucrase → Sucrose → Glucose + Fructose

  • Lactase → Lactose → Glucose + Galactose

Exam Pearl:
Remember the three common disaccharides: Maltose = Glucose + Glucose, Sucrose = Glucose + Fructose, Lactose = Glucose + Galactose.

Physiology 03.question: ১১) Following are examples of endopeptidase excludes..?
Physiology 03.exp:
Endopeptidases hydrolyze internal peptide bonds within a protein molecule, producing smaller peptides. Pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin are classic endopeptidases involved in protein digestion. Pepsin acts in the stomach, whereas trypsin and chymotrypsin act in the small intestine.

In contrast, aminopeptidase is an exopeptidase. It removes amino acids sequentially from the N-terminal (amino end) of peptide chains rather than cleaving internal peptide bonds. Therefore, it is not an endopeptidase.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Endopeptidases: Pepsin, Trypsin, Chymotrypsin, Elastase

  • Exopeptidases: Aminopeptidase, Carboxypeptidase

  • Pepsin: Acts in the stomach.

  • Trypsin & Chymotrypsin: Act in the small intestine.

Exam Pearl:
Endopeptidases cleave internal peptide bonds, whereas exopeptidases remove amino acids from the ends of peptide chains.

Physiology 03.question: ১২) Bile salt helps in absorption of the following except…?
Physiology 03.exp:
Bile salts facilitate the absorption of lipids by forming mixed micelles, which transport lipid digestion products to the intestinal brush border. They are essential for the absorption of long-chain fatty acids, cholesterol, linoleic acid, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K).

Vitamin B12 absorption is independent of bile salts. Instead, vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor (secreted by gastric parietal cells), and the intrinsic factor–B12 complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum via specific receptors.

Therefore, among the given options, Vitamin B12 is the exception.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bile salts aid absorption of:

    • Fatty acids

    • Cholesterol

    • Monoglycerides

    • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

  • Vitamin B12 requires intrinsic factor.

  • Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum.

Exam Pearl:
Bile salts are essential for lipid and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, whereas vitamin B12 absorption depends on intrinsic factor, not bile salts.

Physiology 03.question: ১৩) Liver stores which of the following product?
Physiology 03.exp:
The liver is the principal storage site for vitamin A, where it is stored mainly in hepatic stellate (Ito) cells as retinyl esters. These stores are sufficient to meet the body's requirements for several months. Although the liver stores glucose in the form of glycogen, it does not store free glucose. Bile salts are synthesized by the liver but are mainly conserved through the enterohepatic circulation rather than stored in the liver. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is stored only in small amounts and is not considered a major hepatic storage vitamin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Liver stores:

    • Vitamin A (major storage site)

    • Vitamin D

    • Vitamin B12

    • Iron (as ferritin)

    • Copper

  • Glucose is stored as glycogen, not as free glucose.

  • Bile salts undergo enterohepatic circulation.

Exam Pearl:
The liver is the body's main storage organ for vitamin A; free glucose is not stored—glycogen is.

Physiology 03.question: ১৪) Digestion of CHO doesn’t occur in which of the following?
Physiology 03.exp:
Digestion of carbohydrates (CHO) begins in the oral cavity, where salivary α-amylase (ptyalin) hydrolyzes starch into maltose and dextrins. In the stomach, carbohydrate digestion essentially does not occur because the acidic gastric environment (low pH) rapidly inactivates salivary amylase, and the stomach does not secrete any carbohydrate-digesting enzymes. Carbohydrate digestion resumes in the duodenum with pancreatic amylase and is completed in the small intestine by brush-border enzymes such as maltase, sucrase, and lactase.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Oral cavity: Salivary α-amylase starts starch digestion.

  • Stomach: No significant carbohydrate digestion.

  • Duodenum: Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion.

  • Small intestine: Brush-border enzymes complete carbohydrate digestion to monosaccharides.

Exam Pearl:
Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth, stops in the stomach due to acidic pH, and resumes in the small intestine.

Physiology 03.question: ১৫) Micelle formation is not essential for the absorption of which of the following?
Physiology 03.exp:
Micelle formation is essential for the intestinal absorption of lipid digestion products and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). Bile salts form mixed micelles that transport these hydrophobic substances across the unstirred water layer to the intestinal brush border.

Vitamin B6 is a water-soluble vitamin and is absorbed by simple diffusion or carrier-mediated transport without requiring bile salts or micelle formation. Glycerol is also water-soluble and does not require micelles; however, in standard physiology MCQs, the best single answer is Vitamin B6, as the question contrasts fat-soluble versus water-soluble vitamins.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Micelles are required for absorption of:

    • Vitamin A

    • Vitamin D

    • Vitamin E

    • Vitamin K

    • Long-chain fatty acids

    • Cholesterol

  • Micelles are not required for:

    • Water-soluble vitamins (e.g., Vitamin B6, Vitamin C)

    • Glycerol

    • Short- and medium-chain fatty acids

Exam Pearl:
Bile salt micelles are essential for fat-soluble vitamin absorption, whereas water-soluble vitamins such as Vitamin B6 are absorbed without micelle formation.

Physiology 03.question: ১৬) pH of pancreatic juice is…?
Physiology 03.exp:
Pancreatic juice is a highly alkaline secretion with a pH of approximately 8.0–8.3 due to its high bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) concentration. Bicarbonate is secreted by the pancreatic ductal cells under the influence of secretin. The alkaline pancreatic juice neutralizes the acidic chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach, thereby protecting the duodenal mucosa and providing the optimal pH for the activity of pancreatic enzymes such as trypsin, chymotrypsin, amylase, and lipase.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pancreatic juice pH: 8.0–8.3

  • Secretin stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.

  • CCK stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion.

  • Alkaline pancreatic juice neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum.

Exam Pearl:
Pancreatic juice is strongly alkaline (pH 8.0–8.3) because of its high bicarbonate content.

Physiology 03.question: ১৭) Pepsin is a secretion of which type?
Physiology 03.exp:
Pepsin is a proteolytic enzyme secreted in the stomach. It is not secreted directly; instead, chief cells secrete its inactive precursor, pepsinogen (a zymogen). In the acidic environment of the stomach, hydrochloric acid (HCl) and existing pepsin convert pepsinogen into active pepsin. Pepsin digests proteins by breaking internal peptide bonds, producing smaller peptides.

The question asks about pepsin, not pepsinogen. Therefore, the correct answer is enzyme, while zymogen refers to its inactive precursor.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pepsin = Active proteolytic enzyme

  • Pepsinogen = Inactive zymogen

  • Chief cells → Pepsinogen

  • Parietal (oxyntic) cells → HCl + Intrinsic factor

  • Optimum pH for pepsin: 1.5–2.0

Exam Pearl:
Pepsin is the active gastric enzyme; pepsinogen is its inactive zymogen secreted by chief cells.

Physiology 03.question: ১৮) Which is a typical features of cortical nephron?
Physiology 03.exp:
Cortical nephrons constitute approximately 85% of all nephrons and have their glomeruli located in the outer cortex. They possess short loops of Henle that extend only into the outer medulla. Their primary function is the formation of urine through filtration, reabsorption, and secretion.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Situated in inner cortex → Characteristic of juxtamedullary nephrons.

  • Long loop of Henle → Feature of juxtamedullary nephrons.

  • About 15% of total nephron → Refers to juxtamedullary nephrons, whereas cortical nephrons make up about 85%.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cortical nephrons: ~85%

  • Glomeruli in outer cortex

  • Short loop of Henle

  • Main role: Urine formation

  • Juxtamedullary nephrons: ~15%, long loops of Henle, essential for concentrating urine.

Exam Pearl:
Cortical nephrons are the predominant nephrons (≈85%) with short loops of Henle, while juxtamedullary nephrons are specialized for urine concentration.

Physiology 03.question: ১৯) Which is true about blood flow of nephron?
Physiology 03.exp:
The renal cortex receives the vast majority of renal blood flow, approximately 90–98%, while only 2–10% reaches the renal medulla. This distribution is essential because the cortex contains most of the glomeruli and cortical nephrons, where filtration and the majority of tubular reabsorption occur. The relatively low blood flow to the medulla helps maintain the medullary osmotic gradient, which is necessary for concentrating urine. Increased medullary blood flow would wash out this osmotic gradient and impair urine concentration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renal cortex: Receives ≈90–98% of renal blood flow.

  • Renal medulla: Receives ≈2–10% of renal blood flow.

  • GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (≈180 L/day).

  • Kidneys receive 20–25% of cardiac output.

Exam Pearl:
Nearly all renal blood flow is directed to the cortex; the medulla receives only a small fraction to preserve the corticomedullary osmotic gradient.

Physiology 03.question: ২০) Which is not excretory organ of the body?
Physiology 03.exp:
The urinary bladder is not an excretory organ. Its primary function is to store urine temporarily before micturition. It does not participate in the formation or excretion of metabolic waste.

The other options are involved in excretion:

  • Kidney: Principal excretory organ; removes urea, uric acid, creatinine, excess water, and electrolytes.

  • Respiratory system: Excretes carbon dioxide and water vapor.

  • Intestine: Eliminates substances such as bile pigments, cholesterol, and certain drugs/heavy metals through feces.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kidney: Excretes nitrogenous wastes and regulates fluid-electrolyte balance.

  • Lungs: Excrete CO₂ and water vapor.

  • Skin: Excretes water, salts, and small amounts of urea through sweat.

  • Intestine: Excretes bile pigments and some waste products.

  • Urinary bladder: Stores urine; does not produce or excrete metabolic waste.

Exam Pearl:
The kidney forms urine; the urinary bladder only stores it until voiding.

Physiology 03.question: ২১) Total volume of CSF in adult is..?
Physiology 03.exp:
The total volume of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in a healthy adult is approximately 150 mL. About 25 mL is present within the ventricular system, while approximately 125 mL is located in the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord. CSF is produced mainly by the choroid plexus at a rate of about 500 mL/day, meaning the entire CSF volume is replaced 3–4 times daily. CSF provides mechanical protection, maintains chemical stability, and facilitates the transport of nutrients and waste products within the central nervous system.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Total CSF volume (adult): ≈150 mL

  • CSF production: ≈500 mL/day

  • Major site of production: Choroid plexus

  • CSF turnover: 3–4 times/day

  • Normal lumbar CSF pressure: 70–180 mmH₂O (10–18 cm H₂O)

Exam Pearl:
Remember the pair: CSF volume ≈150 mL; CSF production ≈500 mL/day.

Physiology 03.question: ২২) Urine formation occurs in following steps excludes..?
Physiology 03.exp:
Urine formation occurs through three fundamental processes:

  1. Glomerular filtration – filtration of plasma from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.

  2. Tubular reabsorption – selective movement of water and useful solutes (e.g., glucose, amino acids, sodium) from the renal tubules back into the blood.

  3. Tubular secretion – active transport of substances such as H⁺, K⁺, creatinine, and certain drugs from the blood into the tubular lumen.

There is no physiological process called tubular filtration in renal physiology. Therefore, it is the incorrect option.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Three steps of urine formation:

    • Glomerular filtration

    • Tubular reabsorption

    • Tubular secretion

  • GFR: ≈ 125 mL/min (≈180 L/day)

  • Final urine output: ≈1–2 L/day

Exam Pearl:
Urine formation consists of only three processes: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, and tubular secretion—there is no "tubular filtration."

Physiology 03.question: ২৩) Kidney regulate arterial pressure by..?
Physiology 03.exp:
The kidneys regulate arterial pressure through multiple mechanisms. They secrete renin from the juxtaglomerular cells, activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), which increases blood pressure by vasoconstriction and sodium retention. The kidneys also regulate water reabsorption (under the influence of ADH and RAAS), thereby controlling blood volume and arterial pressure. In addition, they regulate sodium (Na⁺) excretion; increased sodium excretion reduces extracellular fluid volume and lowers blood pressure, whereas sodium retention increases blood pressure. Thus, all the listed mechanisms contribute to arterial pressure regulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renin is secreted by juxtaglomerular cells.

  • RAAS → Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release.

  • Aldosterone → ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption → ↑ water retention → ↑ blood pressure.

  • Long-term arterial pressure regulation depends primarily on renal sodium and water balance.

Exam Pearl:
The kidney is the major long-term regulator of arterial blood pressure through RAAS activation and control of sodium and water excretion.

Physiology 03.question: ২৪) Renal circulation is…?
Physiology 03.exp:
Renal circulation is autoregulated, meaning the kidneys maintain a relatively constant renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) over a wide range of arterial pressures (approximately 80–180 mmHg). This is achieved mainly by the myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback. Autoregulation ensures stable filtration despite fluctuations in systemic blood pressure.

The other options are incorrect:

  • 18% of cardiac output → Renal blood flow is approximately 20–25% of cardiac output.

  • 5 L/min → Normal renal blood flow is about 1.2–1.3 L/min.

  • Decreased in hyperglycemia → Early hyperglycemia (e.g., diabetes mellitus) is usually associated with increased renal blood flow and hyperfiltration, not decreased flow.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renal blood flow (RBF): ≈ 1.2–1.3 L/min (20–25% of cardiac output)

  • Renal plasma flow (RPF): ≈ 600–700 mL/min

  • GFR: ≈ 125 mL/min

  • Autoregulation range: Mean arterial pressure 80–180 mmHg

  • Mechanisms: Myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback

Exam Pearl:
The hallmark of renal circulation is autoregulation, which maintains nearly constant renal blood flow and GFR despite changes in systemic arterial pressure.

Physiology 03.question: ২৫) Glomerular filtration rate is..?
Physiology 03.exp:
The normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy adult is approximately 120–125 mL/min (about 180 L/day). When multiple equivalent values are provided, the best answer is the standard value expressed in mL/min. GFR represents the volume of plasma filtered by all glomeruli per minute and is determined by the filtration pressure, filtration coefficient (Kf), and the integrity of the glomerular filtration barrier. Clinically, GFR is the best overall indicator of renal function and is commonly estimated using creatinine clearance or eGFR equations.

The other options:

  • 124 mL/min – close but not the standard exam value.

  • 7.5 L/hour = 125 mL/min (mathematically correct but less commonly used).

  • 178.5 L/day – approximately 124 mL/min, but not the standard rounded value.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal GFR: 120–125 mL/min

  • Daily filtrate: ≈ 180 L/day

  • Renal blood flow: ≈ 1.2 L/min

  • Renal plasma flow: ≈ 600–700 mL/min

  • Filtration fraction: ≈ 20%

Exam Pearl:
Remember the renal physiology triad: Renal blood flow ≈ 1.2 L/min, GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (≈180 L/day), and filtration fraction ≈20%.

Physiology 03.question: ২৬) Glomerular filtrate becomes hypertonic in which part?
Physiology 03.exp:
The glomerular filtrate becomes hypertonic in the descending limb (DL) of the Loop of Henle. The descending limb is highly permeable to water but relatively impermeable to sodium and other solutes. As the filtrate descends into the hyperosmotic renal medulla, water is reabsorbed by osmosis, increasing the concentration of solutes in the tubular fluid and making it hypertonic.

In contrast, the ascending limb (especially the thick ascending limb) is impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻, causing the tubular fluid to become hypotonic. The proximal tubule reabsorbs water and solutes proportionally, so the filtrate remains isotonic.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Proximal tubule: Isotonic reabsorption.

  • Descending limb: Water permeable → Hypertonic filtrate.

  • Ascending limb: Water impermeable; Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ reabsorption → Hypotonic filtrate.

  • Countercurrent multiplier creates the medullary osmotic gradient.

Exam Pearl:
The descending limb concentrates tubular fluid (hypertonic), whereas the thick ascending limb dilutes it (hypotonic).

Physiology 03.question: ২৭) All of the following are Cause of bence-jones proteinuria excludes..?
Physiology 03.exp:
Bence-Jones proteins are free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) that are filtered by the glomerulus and excreted in the urine. They are classically associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, especially multiple myeloma, and may also be found in conditions such as primary AL amyloidosis and some lymphoproliferative disorders, including certain cases of Hodgkin's disease.

Cushing disease is caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma leading to hypercortisolism and has no association with Bence-Jones proteinuria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bence-Jones proteins: Free κ or λ light chains

  • Most common association: Multiple myeloma

  • May occur in AL amyloidosis and some lymphoproliferative disorders

  • Detected by urine protein electrophoresis or immunofixation

Exam Pearl:
Whenever you see Bence-Jones proteinuria in an MCQ, think first of multiple myeloma.

Physiology 03.question: ২৮) Which one is the Limiting pH of urine?
Physiology 03.exp:
The limiting pH of urine is approximately 4.5, which is the lowest pH that the kidneys can produce under normal physiological conditions. The kidneys acidify urine by secreting H⁺ ions in the distal tubule and collecting duct. Further lowering of urine pH below 4.5 is not possible because the steep H⁺ concentration gradient limits additional hydrogen ion secretion. To continue eliminating acid without reducing urine pH further, H⁺ is excreted as titratable acids (mainly phosphate) and ammonium (NH₄⁺).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal urine pH: 4.5–8.0 (average ≈ 6.0)

  • Limiting (minimum) urine pH: 4.5

  • Major urinary buffers:

    • Phosphate (HPO₄²⁻/H₂PO₄⁻)

    • Ammonia (NH₃/NH₄⁺)

  • Distal nephron is the main site of H⁺ secretion.

Exam Pearl:
The kidney can acidify urine only up to a minimum pH of about 4.5; additional acid is excreted as ammonium and titratable acids.

Physiology 03.question: ২৯) Rothera’s test is positive in which of the following condition??
Physiology 03.exp:
Rothera's test is a qualitative test used to detect ketone bodies (mainly acetoacetate and acetone) in urine. It becomes positive in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a serious complication of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The test is based on the reaction of ketone bodies with sodium nitroprusside in an alkaline medium, producing a purple color.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Diabetic retinopathy – No ketonuria.

  • Diabetes insipidus – Characterized by polyuria due to ADH deficiency/resistance, not ketone production.

  • Diabetic nephropathy – Causes proteinuria, not ketonuria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rothera's test: Detects acetoacetate and acetone.

  • Does not detect β-hydroxybutyrate, the predominant ketone in severe DKA.

  • Positive in: Diabetic ketoacidosis, starvation, prolonged fasting.

  • Principle: Sodium nitroprusside reaction.

Exam Pearl:
A positive Rothera's test indicates ketonuria; in an uncontrolled diabetic, always think of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Physiology 03.question: ৩০) Normal plasma uric level is..mg/dl?
Physiology 03.exp:
The normal plasma (serum) uric acid level in adults is approximately 2–7 mg/dL (slightly higher in men than women). Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism and is excreted primarily by the kidneys. Hyperuricemia may result from increased production or decreased renal excretion and is associated with gout, uric acid nephrolithiasis, and tumor lysis syndrome. Hypouricemia is less common and is usually of limited clinical significance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal serum uric acid: 2–7 mg/dL

  • End product of: Purine metabolism

  • Main route of excretion: Kidneys

  • Hyperuricemia: Seen in gout, chronic kidney disease, tumor lysis syndrome.

  • Xanthine oxidase inhibitors: Allopurinol and febuxostat decrease uric acid production.

Exam Pearl:
Serum uric acid normally ranges from about 2–7 mg/dL; persistent elevation is the biochemical hallmark of hyperuricemia and predisposes to gout.

Physiology 03.question: ৩১) Water turnover in adult is..?
Physiology 03.exp:
Water turnover is the percentage of the body's total water that is replaced each day through intake and loss. In a healthy adult, approximately 2.5 L of water is exchanged daily. Given that total body water is about 60% of body weight (≈42 L in a 70-kg adult), the daily water turnover is approximately 16% of total body water. Infants have a much higher water turnover (40–50%) because of their higher metabolic rate and greater body water content.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adult water turnover: ≈16%/day

  • Infant water turnover: ≈40–50%/day

  • Total body water (adult male): ≈60% of body weight

  • Daily water intake/output: ≈2.5 L

Exam Pearl:
Adults replace about one-sixth (≈16%) of their total body water each day, whereas infants replace nearly half.

Physiology 03.question: ৩২) Body becomes ADH insensitive when ADH concentration exceeds..?
Physiology 03.exp:
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) increases water reabsorption by acting on V₂ receptors in the collecting ducts, promoting insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels. As plasma ADH concentration rises, urine becomes progressively more concentrated. However, once the plasma ADH level reaches approximately 5 pg/mL, the antidiuretic response is maximal, and further increases in ADH produce little or no additional increase in water reabsorption. This is often described in physiology as the kidney becoming functionally insensitive to higher ADH concentrations due to receptor saturation.

The other units (ng/mL, mg/mL, g/mL) are far above physiological ADH concentrations and are incorrect.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal plasma ADH: ~0.5–5 pg/mL

  • Maximal antidiuretic effect: ≈ 5 pg/mL

  • Site of action: Collecting duct (V₂ receptors)

  • Second messenger: cAMP

  • Increases aquaporin-2 insertion into the luminal membrane.

Exam Pearl:
Physiological ADH concentrations are measured in picograms per milliliter (pg/mL); maximal antidiuretic effect occurs at about 5 pg/mL.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৩) Which one is the Main cations in ECF?
Physiology 03.exp:
Sodium (Na⁺) is the principal cation of the extracellular fluid (ECF) and is the major determinant of ECF osmolality and volume. It plays a crucial role in maintaining fluid balance, nerve impulse transmission, muscle contraction, and acid–base balance. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump maintains a high extracellular sodium concentration and a high intracellular potassium concentration.

The other options are incorrect:

  • K⁺ is the principal intracellular cation.

  • Mg²⁺ is mainly an intracellular cation.

  • Al³⁺ has no physiological role as a major body cation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major ECF cation: Na⁺

  • Major ICF cation: K⁺

  • Major ECF anion: Cl⁻

  • Major ICF anions: Phosphates and proteins

  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: Pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP.

Exam Pearl:
Remember the electrolyte pair: Na⁺ dominates the ECF, while K⁺ dominates the ICF.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৪) Which one is not true about the composition of chylomicron?
Physiology 03.exp:
Chylomicrons are the largest and least dense lipoproteins, responsible for transporting dietary triglycerides from the intestine to peripheral tissues. Their composition is predominantly triglycerides (~85–90%), followed by phospholipids (~6–8%), cholesterol (~2–3%), and proteins (~1–2%). The amount of cholesteryl esters in newly formed chylomicrons is very small (typically <1%), not about 2%. Therefore, the statement "Cholesterol ester 2%" is the least accurate and is considered the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Chylomicron composition:

    • Triglycerides: ~85–90%

    • Phospholipids: ~6–8%

    • Cholesterol: ~2–3%

    • Protein: ~1–2%

  • Apolipoprotein B-48: Structural apoprotein of chylomicrons.

  • Lipoprotein lipase (LPL): Hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons.

Exam Pearl:
Chylomicrons are triglyceride-rich lipoproteins; triglycerides constitute nearly 90% of their total lipid content.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৫) Evans blue dye indicator is used for the measurement of......?
Physiology 03.exp:
Evans blue dye (T-1824) is used to measure plasma volume because it binds tightly and almost completely to plasma albumin. Since albumin normally remains within the intravascular compartment, the dye is confined to the plasma, allowing accurate estimation of plasma volume by the indicator dilution principle.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Total body water (TBW): Measured with D₂O (deuterium oxide), ³H₂O, or antipyrine.

  • ECF volume: Measured with inulin, mannitol, or sulfate/thiosulfate.

  • ICF volume: Cannot be measured directly; calculated as TBW − ECF.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Evans blue dye → Plasma volume

  • Radioiodinated albumin (¹²⁵I-albumin) → Plasma volume

  • Inulin/Mannitol → ECF volume

  • D₂O, ³H₂O, Antipyrine → Total body water

  • ICF = TBW − ECF

  • Interstitial fluid = ECF − Plasma volume

Exam Pearl:
Remember the classic indicator: Evans blue binds albumin, so it measures plasma volume—not total body water or extracellular fluid.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৬) How creatinine is produced in the body?
Physiology 03.exp:
Creatinine is produced by the non-enzymatic breakdown of creatine and phosphocreatine in skeletal muscle. Its production occurs at a relatively constant rate and is proportional to an individual's muscle mass. Creatinine is freely filtered by the glomeruli, with minimal tubular secretion, making it a useful endogenous marker of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal function.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Amino acid metabolism primarily produces urea.

  • Nucleic acid (purine) metabolism produces uric acid.

  • Hormone metabolism does not produce creatinine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Creatinine → Derived from creatine/phosphocreatine in muscle.

  • Urea → End product of amino acid metabolism.

  • Uric acid → End product of purine (nucleic acid) metabolism.

  • Serum creatinine is a key indicator of renal function.

Exam Pearl:
Creatinine is a breakdown product of muscle creatine; its constant production makes it an excellent marker of GFR.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৭) Which investigation is done to test filling of the bladder and bladder wall tone?
Physiology 03.exp:
A cystometrogram (CMG) is a urodynamic investigation that assesses the filling phase of the urinary bladder, bladder wall (detrusor) tone, bladder compliance, capacity, and the intravesical pressure-volume relationship. It is the standard test for evaluating bladder function and diagnosing conditions such as neurogenic bladder, overactive bladder, and detrusor instability.

The other options are incorrect:

  • USG evaluates bladder anatomy and residual urine but not bladder tone.

  • IVU (Intravenous urography) assesses the urinary tract radiologically.

  • Cystoscopy provides direct visualization of the bladder mucosa but does not assess bladder filling dynamics or detrusor function.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cystometrogram (CMG): Evaluates bladder filling, capacity, compliance, and detrusor activity.

  • Cystoscopy: Visualizes the bladder and urethra.

  • IVU: Imaging of kidneys, ureters, and bladder after contrast injection.

  • Uroflowmetry: Measures urine flow rate.

Exam Pearl:
Cystometrogram is the investigation of choice for assessing bladder filling, bladder wall tone, and detrusor function.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৮) Autonomic bladder is caused by spinal cord damage above........region?
Physiology 03.exp:
An automatic (reflex/spastic) bladder develops following a spinal cord lesion above the sacral micturition center (S2–S4). Initially, spinal shock causes urinary retention, but after the shock phase, the sacral reflex arc remains intact and micturition occurs reflexly without voluntary control. Thus, bladder emptying becomes automatic in response to bladder filling.

In contrast, a lesion at the sacral segments or pelvic nerves destroys the reflex arc, producing an autonomous (flaccid) bladder, characterized by urinary retention and overflow incontinence.

The term "autonomic bladder" in the question is likely intended to mean "automatic bladder", which is the standard physiology term.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Automatic (reflex/spastic) bladder: Lesion above S2–S4

  • Autonomous (flaccid) bladder: Lesion at S2–S4 or pelvic nerves

  • Sacral micturition center: S2–S4

  • Pontine micturition center: Coordinates normal voiding.

Exam Pearl:
A spinal cord lesion above the sacral micturition center (S2–S4) produces an automatic (reflex) bladder; damage to the sacral center itself produces an autonomous (flaccid) bladder.

Physiology 03.question: ৩৯) Which constituent is highly reabsorbed in renal tubule?
Physiology 03.exp:
Under normal physiological conditions, glucose is almost completely (≈100%) reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule by sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT2 and SGLT1). Therefore, glucose is normally absent from the urine. Although amino acids are also almost completely reabsorbed, the single best answer in standard physiology MCQs is glucose because its reabsorption is a classic example of carrier-mediated transport with a defined transport maximum (Tm).

The other options:

  • Sodium ions: About 99% are reabsorbed, but not completely.

  • Uric acid: Undergoes both reabsorption and secretion; net reabsorption is incomplete.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Glucose: Nearly 100% reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

  • Transporters: SGLT2 (early PCT), SGLT1 (late PCT).

  • Renal threshold for glucose: ≈ 180 mg/dL.

  • Tm for glucose: ≈ 375 mg/min.

Exam Pearl:
Glucose is normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; glycosuria occurs only when the renal threshold or transport maximum is exceeded.

Physiology 03.question: ৪০) Flow to renal medulla is supplied by a specialized portion of peritubular capillary system called......?
Physiology 03.exp:
The vasa recta are specialized straight capillaries arising from the efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons. They descend into the renal medulla alongside the loops of Henle and provide its blood supply. The vasa recta function as countercurrent exchangers, preserving the medullary osmotic gradient essential for concentrating urine while supplying oxygen and nutrients to the medulla. Their slow blood flow minimizes washout of the osmotic gradient.

The other options (vasa medullie, vasa nephri, vasa longa) are not recognized anatomical structures in renal physiology.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Vasa recta: Blood supply to the renal medulla

  • Arise from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons

  • Function as countercurrent exchangers

  • Preserve the medullary osmotic gradient

  • Peritubular capillaries: Surround cortical nephrons and aid reabsorption.

Exam Pearl:
Loop of Henle creates the medullary osmotic gradient (countercurrent multiplier), while the vasa recta preserves it (countercurrent exchanger).

Physiology 03.question: ৪১) Which one increases GFR?
Physiology 03.exp:
Prostaglandins (especially PGE₂ and PGI₂) are renal vasodilators that primarily dilate the afferent arteriole, helping to maintain renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR), particularly during conditions of increased sympathetic activity or hypovolemia. Thus, prostaglandins help preserve GFR.

The other options decrease GFR:

  • Epinephrine → Renal vasoconstriction → ↓ RBF and ↓ GFR.

  • Norepinephrine → Potent vasoconstriction of afferent and efferent arterioles → ↓ GFR.

  • Endothelin → Powerful vasoconstrictor → ↓ RBF and ↓ GFR.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Prostaglandins (PGE₂, PGI₂): Vasodilation → Maintain RBF and GFR

  • NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis → May decrease GFR and precipitate acute kidney injury.

  • Sympathetic stimulation, norepinephrine, epinephrine: Decrease RBF and GFR

  • Endothelin: Potent renal vasoconstrictor → Decreases GFR

Exam Pearl:
Renal prostaglandins protect GFR by dilating the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs block this protective effect and can reduce GFR.

Physiology 03.question: ৪২) A high protein intake is known to.......?
Physiology 03.option3: increase renal blood flow & decrease GFR
Physiology 03.option4: increase GFR & decrease renal blood flow
Physiology 03.exp:
A high-protein intake increases both renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Amino acids stimulate renal vasodilation and enhance tubuloglomerular feedback, leading to afferent arteriolar dilation and an increase in glomerular capillary pressure. This produces glomerular hyperfiltration, a normal physiological response after a protein-rich meal. Persistent hyperfiltration over time may contribute to the progression of chronic kidney disease in susceptible individuals.

The other options are incorrect because a high-protein diet does not decrease renal blood flow or GFR.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • High-protein diet: ↑ Renal blood flow and ↑ GFR

  • Amino acid infusion: Also increases GFR

  • Sympathetic stimulation: ↓ RBF and ↓ GFR

  • Prostaglandins: Help maintain RBF and GFR

  • NSAIDs: May reduce GFR by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis

Exam Pearl:
A protein-rich meal causes physiological renal hyperfiltration—both renal blood flow and GFR increase.

Physiology 03.question: ৪৩) What is the transport maximum for creatinine?
Physiology 03.exp:
This MCQ is testing the transport maximum (Tm) for tubular secretion of creatinine. Although creatinine is primarily eliminated by glomerular filtration, a small amount is secreted by the proximal tubule, and this secretory process has a transport maximum (Tm) of approximately 16 mg/min. Because tubular secretion contributes only minimally under normal conditions, creatinine clearance slightly overestimates the true GFR.

The other options:

  • 375 mg/min → Tm for glucose reabsorption

  • 30 mg/min → Not the Tm for creatinine

  • 15 mg/min → Close, but the accepted exam value is 16 mg/min

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tm for glucose: 375 mg/min

  • Tm for PAH secretion: ≈80 mg/min

  • Tm for creatinine secretion: ≈16 mg/min

  • Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR due to tubular secretion.

Exam Pearl:
Remember the transport maxima: Glucose = 375 mg/min, PAH = 80 mg/min, and creatinine = 16 mg/min.

Physiology 03.question: ৪৪) Which one is secreted by principal cells of distal tubule and collecting tubules?
Physiology 03.exp:
The principal cells of the late distal convoluted tubule and cortical collecting duct primarily reabsorb sodium (Na⁺) through ENaC channels and secrete potassium (K⁺) into the tubular lumen. Aldosterone stimulates these cells by increasing ENaC activity and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, thereby enhancing Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Sodium is reabsorbed, not secreted, by principal cells.

  • Hydrogen (H⁺) is secreted by α-intercalated cells.

  • Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is secreted by β-intercalated cells, not principal cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Principal cells:

    • Reabsorb Na⁺

    • Secrete K⁺

    • Respond to aldosterone and ADH

  • α-Intercalated cells: Secrete H⁺, reabsorb HCO₃⁻ and K⁺

  • β-Intercalated cells: Secrete HCO₃⁻

Exam Pearl:
Principal cells handle sodium and potassium: they reabsorb Na⁺ and secrete K⁺ under the influence of aldosterone.

Physiology 03.question: ৪৫) Tubular fluid/plasma....... concentration ratio can be used to measure water reabsorption by the renal tubule?
Physiology 03.exp:
The tubular fluid/plasma (TF/P) inulin concentration ratio is used to assess water reabsorption by the renal tubules. Inulin is freely filtered at the glomerulus and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the renal tubules. As water is reabsorbed from the tubular fluid, the concentration of inulin in the remaining tubular fluid increases. Therefore, the TF/P inulin ratio rises in proportion to the amount of water reabsorbed, making it an ideal marker for studying tubular water handling.

The other options are incorrect:

  • PAH is filtered and actively secreted; used to estimate renal plasma flow.

  • Antipyrine is used to measure total body water.

  • Thiosulphate is used to measure extracellular fluid volume.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Inulin clearance → Gold standard for GFR

  • TF/P inulin ratio → Assesses tubular water reabsorption

  • PAH clearance → Estimates renal plasma flow (RPF)

  • Antipyrine/D₂O → Total body water (TBW)

  • Inulin: Freely filtered, not reabsorbed, not secreted

Exam Pearl:
Inulin is the ideal renal marker because it is filtered only; therefore, its TF/P concentration ratio directly reflects the extent of water reabsorption along the nephron.

Physiology 03.question: ৪৬) Which hormone acts on collecting tubule & duct?
Physiology 03.exp:
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) primarily acts on the late distal tubule and collecting ducts, especially the principal cells, by binding to V₂ receptors. This activates the cAMP pathway, leading to insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the luminal membrane, thereby increasing water reabsorption, concentrating the urine, and reducing urine volume.

Although aldosterone also acts on the late distal tubule and collecting duct to increase Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion, the classic single-best answer for the hormone acting on the collecting tubule and duct in relation to water handling is ADH.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ADH: Acts on V₂ receptors in collecting ducts → ↑ Aquaporin-2 → ↑ Water reabsorption.

  • Aldosterone: Acts on principal cells → ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption, ↑ K⁺ secretion.

  • ANP: Decreases Na⁺ reabsorption and antagonizes RAAS.

  • PTH: Acts mainly on the proximal and distal tubules, increasing Ca²⁺ reabsorption and phosphate excretion.

Exam Pearl:
ADH is the principal hormone regulating water permeability of the collecting duct through insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.

Physiology 03.question: ৪৭) FF = ?
Physiology 03.exp:
Filtration fraction (FF) is defined as the fraction of renal plasma flow (RPF) that is filtered through the glomeruli. It is calculated as:

FF = GFR / RPF

In a healthy adult:

  • GFR ≈ 125 mL/min

  • RPF ≈ 625 mL/min

  • Therefore, FF ≈ 125/625 = 0.20 (20%).

Filtration fraction is influenced by changes in afferent and efferent arteriolar resistance and is an important indicator of glomerular hemodynamics.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Filtration Fraction (FF) = GFR / RPF

  • Normal FF: ≈ 20% (0.20)

  • GFR: ≈ 125 mL/min

  • RPF: ≈ 600–700 mL/min

  • Renal blood flow (RBF): ≈ 1.2 L/min

Exam Pearl:
Remember the renal physiology triad: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min, RPF ≈ 625 mL/min, and FF ≈ 20% (GFR/RPF).

Physiology 03.question: ৪৮) Tubular fluid in distal & collecting tubules is further diluted......?
Physiology 03.exp:
The tubular fluid entering the distal tubule is already hypotonic because the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle reabsorbs NaCl but is impermeable to water. In the absence of ADH, the late distal tubule and collecting ducts remain relatively impermeable to water. Sodium continues to be reabsorbed, but water cannot follow, so the tubular fluid becomes further diluted, resulting in the excretion of large volumes of dilute urine.

In the presence of ADH, water permeability increases due to insertion of aquaporin-2 channels, causing water reabsorption and formation of concentrated urine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • No ADH: Collecting ducts impermeable to water → Dilute urine

  • ADH present: ↑ Aquaporin-2 → Concentrated urine

  • Thick ascending limb: "Diluting segment" (reabsorbs NaCl, impermeable to water)

  • Minimum urine osmolality: ~50 mOsm/kg

  • Maximum urine osmolality: ~1200 mOsm/kg

Exam Pearl:
Absence of ADH produces the most dilute urine because water cannot be reabsorbed from the distal nephron, while solute reabsorption continues.

Physiology 03.question: ৪৯) Which one does not increases thirst?
Physiology 03.exp:
Thirst is stimulated primarily by increased plasma osmolality, angiotensin II, and dryness of the mouth and pharynx. Increased plasma osmolality activates hypothalamic osmoreceptors, while angiotensin II directly stimulates the thirst center during hypovolemia or hypotension. Dryness of the mouth also promotes the sensation of thirst.

In contrast, increased blood pressure suppresses thirst because it is usually associated with an increase in effective circulating volume. Stretch receptors in the cardiovascular system inhibit the thirst center, reducing the drive to drink water.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Stimuli for thirst:

    • ↑ Plasma osmolality (most potent)

    • ↑ Angiotensin II

    • ↓ Blood volume/↓ Blood pressure

    • Dry mouth and pharynx

  • ADH and thirst are both stimulated by hyperosmolality.

  • Increased blood pressure/volume inhibits thirst.

Exam Pearl:
The strongest physiological stimulus for thirst is increased plasma osmolality, whereas increased blood pressure suppresses the thirst mechanism.

Physiology 03.question: ৫০) Segmentation contraction is the movement of the......?
Physiology 03.exp:
Segmentation contractions are the characteristic mixing movements of the small intestine. They occur due to rhythmic contraction of the circular smooth muscle, dividing the intestinal contents into small segments and repeatedly mixing chyme with digestive enzymes and bringing it into close contact with the intestinal mucosa for efficient digestion and absorption. Unlike peristalsis, segmentation produces little or no net forward movement of intestinal contents.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Stomach: Primarily exhibits mixing waves and peristaltic contractions.

  • Large intestine: Shows haustral contractions and mass movements.

  • Oesophagus: Propels food by peristalsis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Segmentation: Characteristic of the small intestine

  • Function: Mixing, not propulsion

  • Peristalsis: Propulsive movement throughout the GI tract

  • Haustral contractions: Mixing movement of the large intestine

  • Mass movements: Propel feces in the colon

Exam Pearl:
Segmentation is the principal mixing movement of the small intestine, whereas peristalsis is the principal propulsive movement of the gastrointestinal tract.
